transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-04-14
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Alyssa Chen (Redwood AE); Marcus Ortega (Redwood SE); Daniel Park (Redwood Solutions Eng); Raj Patel (VeraMed ML Platform Lead); Sophie Turner (VeraMed CTO); Ellen Wu (VeraMed SRE); Tomás Rivera (VeraMed Product)

Summary:
Quick scoping to translate VeraMed's operational workload into measurable SLOs (TTFT vs TPOT), pick p95/p99 targets, and agree a measurement and benchmark plan for the POC. Discussed traffic profile, payload variance, acceptable fallbacks, and security constraints (VPC/KMS/SOC2). Determined action items and schedule for benchmark dry-run and acceptance criteria.

Topics Covered:
- Definition tradeoffs: TTFT (time-to-first-token) vs TPOT (total-per-token) and when each matters
- SLO targets (p95/p99) across classes of requests (short chat, long summarization, embeddings)
- Workload sizing: concurrency, burstiness, tail requests, token length distributions
- Measurement plan: sampling, synthetic vs production replays, cold vs warm cache runs
- Infrastructure choices: hosted vs dedicated vs private VPC pilot; KMS and audit log needs

Action items: see metadata list above.

Transcript Body:
[00:00:12] Alyssa (Redwood AE): ok thanks everybody for joining, um we'll go 60-ish minutes, try to land SLOs and next steps. Marcus will kick with the perf assumptions.
[00:00:27] Marcus (Redwood SE): cool hi y'all. So quick context, we're trying to map your current request types to which latency metric matters. typically for interactive chat you care about TTFT, for batch summarization TPOT sometimes more relevant. but there are hybrids.
[00:00:45] Raj (VeraMed): yeah for our clinicians chat flow the perceived latency is first token, they need a quick response to keep the conversation going. but for our nightly summarizer it's okay if individual requests take longer as long as throughput is high and cost stays contained.
[00:01:10] Sophie (CTO): can you explain the exact difference so my PMs and SREs line up on acceptance criteria? i keep seeing both metrics in your docs.
[00:01:20] Marcus: sure, short version: TTFT = time to first token after request arrives, which is dominated by scheduling, cold startup, kv cache misses, and attention kernel warmups. TPOT = total per token, essentially (total latency)/(number of tokens) aggregated — gives you per-token cost and user-perceived overall time for long outputs. p95/p99 apply to either metric depending on which user journey you're protecting.
[00:01:45] Tomás (Product): for our triage chat we want p95 TTFT under 250ms and p99 under 600ms as targets. is that realistic on your hosted plane?
[00:01:58] Marcus: 250ms p95 is tight but achievable for short prompts on dedicated or well-configured hosted with warm KV caches and batching disabled for low-latency routes. key unknowns: prompt prefix size, avg seq len, and arrival concurrency. if you have lots of concurrent users we recommend dedicated pools.
[00:02:18] Ellen (SRE): we have peaks of 120 rps for chat during rounds, 75 avg across the day. sequences are usually 16-48 tokens for chat, but the summarizer hits 800-1200 tokens.
[00:02:35] Marcus: that's useful. so we'd map traffic into buckets: short-chat (<64 tokens), medium-gen (64-512), long-batch (>512). each bucket gets separate SLOs and sampling rules.
[00:02:50] Alyssa: quick question on measurement: do you want synthetic clients hitting hosted endpoints or do you prefer replaying real production traces?
[00:02:58] Raj: we can do both, but replay is ideal — it shows cache behavior. we can extract 72 hours of anonymized traces.
[00:03:10] Marcus: perfect. for replay we need: timestamp, payload size, seq length, response token count, and an indicator if user expects streaming. that lets us measure TTFT and TPOT faithfully.
[00:03:28] Speaker 1 (?): there's also the cold start scenario to consider, right, like first request after model swap or instance spin up?
[00:03:35] Marcus: yes, two measurement modes: warm (steady-state with KV caches and warmed instances) and cold (simulate rolling deployment or scale-up events). we'll capture both and surface separate SLOs and remediation recommendations.
[00:03:50] Sophie: for acceptance, we probably want TTFT p95 <= 300ms for chat and p99 <= 700ms across warm runs; cold start allowance can be higher but should be documented. does that sound reasonable?
[00:04:05] Marcus: yes that's within reason for dedicated or private with right sizing. hosted might hit p95 300-350ms depending on region and multi-tenant variance.
[00:04:18] Tomás: for summarization what's the TPOT target? we don't have a per-token cost threshold yet.
[00:04:25] Daniel (Redwood SE): for long gen we propose a TPOT baseline of 12-18ms/token p95 depending on quantization and instance family. with int8 quant and batch optimizations we can cut that. TPOT p99 will be 2-3x p95 in worst tail cases without batching control.
[00:04:45] Raj: hmm okay budget-wise we want to keep average token cost under $0.0008 per token in pilot. can you translate TPOT latency to expected cost?
[00:04:55] Marcus: we can estimate cost based on tokens/sec and instance hourly price; we'll provide a cost-per-token worksheet. that's part of Marcus's perf doc.
[00:05:05] Ellen: security: we must run in VPC peered env with KMS-managed keys and audit trails. private deployment is our preference but initial POC can be in dedicated with VPC peering.
[00:05:20] Alyssa: we can do dedicated behind your VPC peering and provide SOC2 artifacts, audit logs, and KMS integrations. we'll include a short runbook for the KMS handshake.
[00:05:34] Sophie: what about traffic shaping during benchmark to emulate spikes? we have burstiness from emergency workflows.
[00:05:42] Marcus: we'll produce traffic scripts that can reproduce burst patterns and tail events — staircase, sudden up, slow ramp. sampling plan recommends 3 runs per pattern: warm steady state, cold deployment, and burst stress.
[00:05:58] Tomás: how do we set p99 thresholds when bursts cause queuing? do we allow queuing > SLO if queueing is in our control?
[00:06:08] Marcus: good question — SLO should be defined inclusive of system behavior. we recommend p99 measured at the ingress of Redwood's runtime (so excludes network transit within your VPC) and define a policy: if we detect queuing due to upstream throttles, we mark those samples as backlog-affected and surface them separately. acceptance will define an allowed % of backlog-affected samples in a 24-hr window.
[00:06:30] Raj: what's a typical allowed %?
[00:06:33] Marcus: for pilots we often allow up to 1% p99 violations, with an additional 1-2% backlog-affected tolerance for bursts. final numbers can be negotiated.
[00:06:45] Ellen: instrumentation — do you add traces/tags so our SREs can correlate?
[00:06:50] Daniel: yes, we emit tracing headers and per-request metadata (model_version, instance_id, cache_hit) that you can ship to your observability. we'll share the schema.
[00:07:02] Speaker 2 (customer): and how long does the POC run?
[00:07:06] Alyssa: typical pilot is 3-4 weeks: week 0 setup & connectivity, week 1 dry runs + tuning, week 2 full runs + sampling, week 3 wrap + acceptance. we can compress if you provide fast access to traffic and infra.
[00:07:20] Sophie: timeline looks good. we need pilot-ready by May 10th ideally.
[00:07:24] Marcus: to hit May 10th we need the traffic export by Apr 20 and a short access window for VPC peering by Apr 22.
[00:07:32] Raj: we can commit to that.
[00:07:35] Tomás: what are acceptance criteria besides p95/p99?
[00:07:40] Marcus: acceptance is multi-dimensional: SLOs per bucket (TTFT/TPOT p95 and p99), correctness/regression checks using your eval prompts (we'll run n=5000 sample comparisons), and cost envelope validation. plus security checklist (VPC, KMS, audit log accessible).
[00:07:55] Alyssa: we'll provide a pilot acceptance doc with checkboxes.
[00:07:59] Raj: any gotchas around KV cache warmup skewing TTFT?
[00:08:03] Marcus: yes, warm-up matters; measurement plan includes a warmup phase to stabilize KV caches, then sampling windows. we'll also run artificially-cold iterations to quantify impact.
[00:08:18] Sophie: if we see regressions on quality after quantization, what's the rollback policy?
[00:08:23] Marcus: we always recommend a canary and automatic rollback based on eval regressions. the runtime can route a percentage to a higher-precision variant if quality drops beyond threshold.
[00:08:35] Ellen: who runs the benchmark harness? our team or Redwood?
[00:08:39] Alyssa: Redwood will run the initial harness in your environment (dedicated pool with VPC peering). we'll provide the repo and scripts and train your SREs to run them. final runs can be automated in your CI.
[00:08:52] Tomás: do you support streaming measurement for TTFT when tokens stream in?
[00:08:58] Marcus: yes, we instrument first-byte timings for streaming and measure TTFT there; we'll need an indicator in the trace to mark streaming sessions.
[00:09:06] Raj: OK, let's document the SLO matrix now quickly for clarity.
[00:09:10] Marcus: proposed SLO matrix (rough draft):
 - short-chat (<64 tokens): TTFT p95 <= 250ms, p99 <= 600ms (warm); cold p95 <= 800ms
 - medium-gen (64-512 tokens): TTFT p95 <= 400ms, TPOT p95 <= 15ms/token; p99 targets 2x p95
 - long-batch (>512 tokens): TPOT p95 <= 20ms/token, throughput target 250 tokens/sec per pool node (subject to hw), p99 considered separately
[00:09:45] Sophie: those seem reasonable as starting points. we'll push back if costs blow up.
[00:09:50] Marcus: under- stood. we'll provide a cost sensitivity table.
[00:09:55] Daniel: measurement plan outline: 1) ingest traffic export; 2) sanitize and sample per SLO buckets; 3) run warm-up; 4) execute 3 patterns (steady, cold-deploy, burst) with 3 repeats each; 5) collect per-request telemetry and compute TTFT and TPOT p95/p99; 6) run quality evals against your golden prompts.
[00:10:18] Raj: how big should the sampled set be for reliable p99 estimates?
[00:10:22] Marcus: p99 is sensitive — we recommend at least 10000 samples per bucket for stable p99 estimation, or use bootstrapping if sample counts are low. we'll provide guidance.
[00:10:35] Tomás: what about tail noise introduced by multi-tenancy in hosted?
[00:10:40] Marcus: hosted will have more variance; dedicated/private gives predictable tails. we'll quantify variance in the pilot and recommend a routing rule to fallback to a larger model variant or different region during tail events.
[00:10:55] Speaker 3 (customer): competitor question — how does this compare to LambdaBench?
[00:10:58] Alyssa: LambdaBench focuses on raw throughput lab benchmarks; Redwood's differentiator is production-aware SLOs, KV caching, and integrated rollouts + canaries. we'll share a short competitive note.
[00:11:12] Sophie: ok let's align on deliverables and deadlines.
[00:11:16] Alyssa: deliverables -> benchmark harness link, sample traffic spec, SLO matrix doc, cost worksheet, pilot acceptance checklist. deadlines in next-steps.
[00:11:27] Raj: one more thing — we may need to involve security/compliance for KMS approvals; expect them to request docs.
[00:11:33] Alyssa: we'll send SOC2/ISO docs and a short integration guide.
[00:11:37] Marcus: i'll attach the perf knobs and recommended instance families.
[00:11:40] Ellen: thanks, that's helpful.
[00:11:45] Alyssa: ok final recap: VeraMed will send trace and prompt samples by Apr 20, Redwood will share benchmark repo and docs by Apr 18, schedule dry-run week of Apr 25, pilot aiming May 10. action owners in the metadata.
[00:11:60] (several people): thanks, bye.
